expectedText:
CALIFORNIA GENERAL WHISTLEBLOWER PROTECTION (LABOR CODE SECTION 1102.5) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Corp.

INTERNAL REPORTING CHANNEL
Acme Corp. provides the following channel(s) for Jordan Lee to report information the employee has reasonable cause to believe discloses a violation of a state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation: _______________________________________________. Using an internal channel is not required by the statute addressed in this document, which independently protects a report made instead — or also — to a government or law enforcement agency, or to another person or employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance.

PROTECTED DISCLOSURES: WHAT COUNTS, AND TO WHOM
California law prohibits an employer, or anyone acting on the employer's behalf, from making, adopting, or enforcing any rule, regulation, or policy that would prevent an employee from disclosing information to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, or to another employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct a violation, or from providing information to or testifying before any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry. This protection applies whenever the employee has reasonable cause to believe the information discloses a violation of a state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation — regardless of whether making that kind of disclosure is part of the employee's own job duties. A report a government-agency employee makes to their own employer counts as a disclosure to a government or law enforcement agency for these same purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not make, adopt, or enforce any rule, regulation, or policy preventing an employee from disclosing information to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, or to another employee who has authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or from providing information to, or testifying before, any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the information discloses a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "A report made by an employee of a government agency to their employer is a disclosure of information to a government or law enforcement agency pursuant to subdivisions (a) and (b)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  Known gap: Both citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(a) and § 1102.5(e) — disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. The 'reasonable cause to believe' standard quoted here is drawn directly from this statutory text; this clause does not add independent case law interpreting how courts apply that standard to particular facts, and no such corroborating authority was verified in this research pass. This clause does not itself determine that any specific disclosure, or its actual recipient, falls within this statute's protection in a specific case, and does not address California's separate, narrower securities-fraud-specific whistleblower statutes or the distinct federal Sarbanes-Oxley/Dodd-Frank protections addressed elsewhere in this corpus.

THE ANTI-RETALIATION RULE ITSELF
Separately from prohibiting rules or policies that would block a protected disclosure, this same statute independently prohibits an employer, or anyone acting on the employer's behalf, from retaliating against an employee for making a protected disclosure — or because the employer believes the employee disclosed or may disclose that kind of information — to any of the same recipients: a government or law enforcement agency, a person with authority over the employee, or another employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or in providing information to or testifying before an investigating public body. The same reasonable-cause-to-believe standard, and the same rule that this protection applies regardless of the employee's job duties, govern this anti-retaliation prohibition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for disclosing information, or because the employer believes that the employee disclosed or may disclose information, to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee or another employee who has the authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or for providing information to, or testifying before, any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the information discloses a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  Known gap: This clause's citation is to a single statutory subdivision, Labor Code § 1102.5(b) — the anti-retaliation prohibition itself, distinct from the rule-and-policy prohibition of subdivision (a) addressed in a separate clause of this document. Separately, on verification: this section, as currently codified and as most recently amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 612 (SB 497), effective January 1, 2024, does not itself contain a rebuttable presumption of retaliation for adverse action taken within a set number of days of the protected activity. Fetching and comparing the current statutory text confirmed this directly, and the bill's own Legislative Counsel's Digest confirms it as well: the 90-day rebuttable presumption created by SB 497 was enacted into a companion statute, Labor Code § 98.6 (and, per that same digest, into Labor Code § 1197.5), while SB 497's amendment to § 1102.5 itself changed only the civil-penalty structure addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not state, and does not cite, a 90-day presumption as part of § 1102.5, because none exists in the fetched text of this section; a reader whose situation might involve a wage claim or a complaint within the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction may find that presumption addressed under Labor Code § 98.6 in this corpus's separate Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet.

REFUSING TO BREAK THE LAW, AND PROTECTION CARRIED FROM A FORMER JOB
The same statute also prohibits an employer from retaliating against an employee for refusing to participate in an activity that would violate a state or federal statute, or that would violate or fail to comply with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation. It separately prohibits retaliation against an employee for having exercised these same protections while working for a previous employer, not only the current one.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for refusing to participate in an activity that would result in a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for having exercised their rights under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) in any former employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  Known gap: Both citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(c) and § 1102.5(d) — disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. This clause does not itself determine that any specific refusal, or any specific prior-employment activity, actually falls within this statute's coverage in a particular case.

WHAT THIS STATUTE DOES NOT REACH, AND WHO COUNTS AS AN "EMPLOYER"
This statute does not apply to rules, regulations, or policies implementing — or to employer action against an employee who violates — the lawyer-client privilege, the physician-patient privilege, or the confidentiality of trade secret information. Separately, this statute prohibits retaliation against an employee because that employee is a family member of someone who has engaged in, or is perceived to have engaged in, activity this statute protects. And for purposes of this statute, "employer" is defined broadly enough to include a client employer in certain labor-contracting relationships, and certain employers as defined for workplace safety purposes, not only an employee's own direct employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This section does not apply to rules, regulations, or policies that implement, or to actions by employers against employees who violate, the confidentiality of the lawyer-client privilege of Article 3 (commencing with Section 950) of, or the physician-patient privilege of Article 6 (commencing with Section 990) of, Chapter 4 of Division 8 of the Evidence Code, or trade secret information."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(g) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "An employer, or a person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee because the employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in any acts protected by this section."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "For purposes of this section, “employer” or “a person acting on behalf of the employer” includes, but is not limited to, a client employer as defined in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 2810.3 and an employer listed in subdivision (b) of Section 6400."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  Known gap: All three citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(g), (h), and (i) — disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. Subdivision (i)'s definition of covered "employer" cross-references Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1) (the client-employer definition) and § 6400(b); this document quotes only § 1102.5(i)'s own text making that cross-reference and does not independently fetch or verify the text of § 2810.3 or § 6400 themselves. This clause does not determine that any specific privilege, trade-secret, family-relationship, or multi-employer fact pattern actually falls within or outside this statute's scope in a particular case.

CIVIL PENALTY AND ATTORNEY'S FEES UNDER THIS STATUTE
In addition to any other available remedy, California law makes an employer who violates this statute liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation, awarded to the employee who was retaliated against. In assessing the amount of that penalty, the Labor Commissioner considers the nature and seriousness of the violation based on the evidence obtained during the investigation, including the type of violation, the economic or mental harm suffered, and the chilling effect on the exercise of employment rights in the workplace. Separately, a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful action for a violation of this statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In addition to other remedies available, an employer is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per employee for each violation of this section to be awarded to the employee who was retaliated against."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "In assessing this penalty, the Labor Commissioner shall consider the nature and seriousness of the violation based on the evidence obtained during the course of the investigation. The Labor Commissioner’s consideration of the nature and seriousness of the violation shall include, but is not limited to, the type of violation, the economic or mental harm suffered, and the chilling effect on the exercise of employment rights in the workplace, and shall be considered to the extent evidence obtained during the investigation concerned any of these or other relevant factors."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  "The court is authorized to award reasonable attorney’s fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful action for a violation of these provisions."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(j) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1102.5.)
  Known gap: All three citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(1), (f)(2), and (j) — disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. The $10,000 figure is a per-employee, per-violation cap the Labor Commissioner may assess after considering the listed factors; it is not an amount awarded automatically or in every case. This same statutory text is also cited, for the same civil-penalty and fee-shifting mechanics, in this corpus's separate Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet, which addresses this statute in the context of an already-ended employment relationship; this clause states the identical statutory mechanics for a reader who is still employed. This clause does not itself determine that any specific violation occurred, or that any specific penalty or fee award would result, in a particular case.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge that you have received and read this document.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Company: Acme Corp.
Date: September 4, 2026
City, State: Sacramento, California
